AI-assisted decisions: guardrails, human review and the kill switch

After this lesson you can:
  • Explain how model outputs may lawfully influence a credit decision
  • Describe the kill switch and what 'degrade to human review' means
  • Summarise the governance around models and AI agents

Learning rhythm: read one section at a time, pause to explain the control in your own words, then answer the knowledge check without looking back.

On this page
  1. AI proposes; policy and humans dispose
  2. The kill switch is a product control
  3. Fairness is testable
  4. Regulatory anchors
  5. Where this lives in LoanOS
  6. Knowledge check

1. AI proposes; policy and humans dispose

Scorecards and ML models are useful — and regulated.

LoanOS's design keeps them in their lane: a model's output enters a decision only as a provenance-tagged fact ('model X version Y scored 0.71 on these inputs at this time'), which the deterministic policy then weighs.

Models never call the shots directly, and material AI influence triggers mandatory human review — an underwriter confirms before the outcome stands.

Every model that materially affects decisions — vendor models and clever spreadsheets included — sits in a model inventory with an owner, use case, version, validation evidence, fairness/performance monitoring and a risk tier.

2. The kill switch is a product control

When a model misbehaves — drift, bias, a bad release — the RE needs to stop it now, not at the next deployment.

The kill switch does that: model-scoped or global, it blocks runtime model use immediately, records who pulled it and why, and degrades affected decisions to manual review — fail closed, never fail open.

Draft RBI model-risk guidance points exactly this way: inventory, validation, human oversight, override controls.

Agentic AI gets the same treatment with tighter bounds: digital workers are proposal-only, tenant-scoped, guardrail-checked before every action, and approving their material actions requires authenticated humans. Module 9 goes deeper.

3. Fairness is testable

The FREE-AI committee's principles — fairness, explainability, accountability, resilience — translate into artefacts a BA can demand: cohort-level performance and fairness reports, explainability evidence for adverse decisions, red-team results for generative systems, incident processes with affected-decision identification. If a vendor cannot produce these, the model does not belong in a credit path.

Regulatory anchors

  • RBI-MRM-DRAFT-2026 — Model inventory, validation, human oversight and kill-switch controls.
  • FREE-AI-2025 — Fairness, accountability, explainability, resilience — the principles behind the artefacts.
  • INDIA-AI-GOV-2025 — Cross-sector AI governance guidance layered under RBI directions.

Family IDs resolve in the India regulatory register (docs/compliance/india-regulatory-register.md), which owns sources and caveats.

Where this lives in LoanOS

  • Capability AIG-008 — Global, model, workflow and use-case kill switches.
  • Capability AIG-010 — Human review, customer disclosure and human handoff.
  • Capability AIG-014 — Decision reason lineage from the actual deciding authority.
  • Code packages/core/src/ai/model-governance.js — Kill-switch state source of truth; the decision engine enforces it.

Knowledge check

Answer aloud or write your choice before opening the explanation. If you miss it, revisit the named section—not the whole lesson.

1. The kill switch is activated for the income-estimation model. What happens to in-flight applications that depend on it?

  1. They auto-approve on last known scores
  2. They fail with errors
  3. They degrade to manual review — the human queue picks them up
  4. They are cancelled
Reveal answer and reasoning

C. Kill-switch semantics are fail-closed-to-humans: model-dependent decisions route to review rather than proceeding on stale or absent model output.

2. How does a model's opinion legally enter a LoanOS credit decision?

  1. The model API is called from the engine at evaluation time
  2. As a provenance-tagged fact evaluated by deterministic policy
  3. Via a webhook that sets the outcome
  4. It doesn't — models are banned
Reveal answer and reasoning

B. Facts in, deterministic policy over them — with material AI influence forcing human review. The engine itself never performs I/O.
